system.name: Skyloft
system.one_liner: a general, high-efficiency user-space scheduling framework that uses user-mode interrupts for microsecond-scale preemption

components.name: Skyloft LibOS
components.role: user-space library OS providing kernel-bypass scheduling with POSIX-compatible APIs

components.name: I/O stack
components.role: handles I/O interrupts in user space and feeds events into Uthread scheduling

components.name: Shared runqueues
components.role: hold runnable user threads, color-coded per application

components.name: UINTR handler
components.role: handles user-mode (UINTR) interrupts and feeds events into Uthread scheduling

components.name: Uthread scheduling
components.role: core user-thread scheduler that selects and switches runnable uthreads

components.name: Scheduling Policy
components.role: pluggable scheduling interface (task_enqueue/dequeue/block/wakeup) invoked by Uthread scheduling

components.name: Skyloft Kernel Module
components.role: kernel-space module managing kthread switching between applications and other privileged operations

components.name: Timer source
components.role: hardware timer whose interrupts are delivered directly to user space via UINTR

components.name: I/O device
components.role: physical I/O device whose interrupts are delivered directly to the I/O stack

components.name: CPU
components.role: isolated core (shown twice) running one active kernel thread for one application while holding another application's thread inactive

flows.what: I/O interrupt delivered directly to user space

content.key_idea: Skyloft splits scheduling into a user-space LibOS (uthread scheduling, shared runqueues, I/O stack, UINTR handling) and a minimal kernel module, using user-mode interrupts and isolated cores so each app's active kernel thread runs without kernel-scheduler interference.
content.reading_order: Follow circled steps 1-5: Scheduling Policy into Uthread scheduling, out to Shared runqueues and Skyloft Kernel Module, then Timer source and I/O device up into UINTR handler and I/O stack.

Single Binding Rule: No two or more active kernel threads may be bound to the same isolated core simultaneously.
every application has one active kernel thread occupying distinct isolated cores

summary: Skyloft is a general, high-efficiency user-space scheduling framework that uses user-mode interrupts (UINTR) to deliver hardware timer and I/O events directly to user space, enabling microsecond-scale preemption. Figure 3 splits Skyloft into two components: the Skyloft LibOS in user space, bundling an I/O stack, a UINTR handler, Shared runqueues, and a central Uthread scheduling module driven by a pluggable Scheduling Policy interface; and the Skyloft Kernel Module in kernel space, which performs privileged kthread switches. Five circled numbers trace the control flow: policy calls into the scheduler (1), uthread and kthread switches to the runqueues and kernel module (2, 3), and timer/I/O interrupts into the UINTR handler and I/O stack (4, 5). Two CPU boxes below use blue and green to show each isolated core running one active thread for App 1 or App 2, with the other's thread inactive, illustrating the Single Binding Rule.
summary_zh: 图3示Skyloft架构：用户空间LibOS含I/O栈、UINTR处理器、共享运行队列与Uthread调度，由调度策略驱动；内核空间模块负责kthread切换。底部CPU用蓝绿区分App1、App2的活跃线程。
notes: layout-proposal: hub-and-layered — a central Uthread scheduling hub wired to five surrounding LibOS components (I/O stack, UINTR handler, runqueues, scheduling policy, kernel module), itself sitting atop a user-space/kernel-space layered split down to timer/I/O hardware and CPUs; named template 'layered' captures the privilege-level stack but not the hub-like wiring around Uthread scheduling.
